title: Ivan's rebellion
hookLine: in Dostoevsky, Ivan refuses a harmony bought with a child's tears (The Brothers Karamazov, book 5)

cards: A small-town tavern, and two brothers at a table. The younger, Alyosha, is a novice at the local monastery, gentle, a listener.

The older, Ivan, is brilliant and restless, and tonight he says out loud what he really thinks. He's been collecting things, he tells his brother: clippings, stories. And he isn't going to argue about whether God exists.
He's going to argue about something harder. This is Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov, and the chapter is called Rebellion.

teach.b: First, the collection. Ivan has been gathering true stories of cruelty done to children. He tells several.
They're too hard to repeat here, and that's his point. The grown-ups, he says, have eaten the apple, so to speak; let them answer for it. But the children haven't.
Why should they suffer? Second, the refusal. Ivan imagines the end of everything: every wrong explained, everyone embracing, a harmony where all is made right.
And he doesn't want it, if it costs one child's tears. It isn't worth that price. He's careful: it isn't God he refuses, he says.
He just, most respectfully, returns his ticket. Alyosha quietly names it: that's rebellion. Third, the question.
Ivan turns it on his brother.

teach.h: WOULD YOU BUILD IT ON ONE CHILD?
teach.b: Suppose you were building the world, to make people happy at last, and it could only be done by torturing one small child. Would you agree to be the builder on those terms?
Tell the truth. And Alyosha, the novice, answers softly: no, I wouldn't consent. Fourth, what the book does next.
Alyosha doesn't win the argument. He speaks of one who can forgive everything, because he gave his own innocent blood. Ivan answers with a long poem about a Grand Inquisitor.
When it ends, Alyosha doesn't rebut it. He leans over and kisses his brother.
Dostoevsky lets the question stand at full strength, in the mouth of a character he gave strong arguments. This block has listened to Job, the cross, the Quran's patience, Julian's promise.
Ivan is the voice that says: not at that price. The novel gives him his full say, and so does this day.

how: Readers, believers and unbelievers alike, return to Ivan's chapter when they think about the problem of suffering, and it's read in literature, philosophy and theology classes.

o: a plot by Ivan to overthrow the Russian tsar
a young monk's protest against his monastery
refusing a harmony bought with one child's tears

games.q: you're Alyosha. Ivan asks: if you could build a world where everyone is happy at last, but only by torturing one small child, would you agree to build it?
o: yes, if the end is good enough.
games.why: Alyosha, the novice, answers softly: no. and the novel doesn't hand him an argument that makes Ivan's question go away.

practice: Pick one hard question you can't answer, one you can hold for two minutes: why that happened to them, why it goes on.
Hold it like a stone in your open hand, and each time the mind reaches for an answer or for the exit, notice, and set the question gently back in your palm.
You're not solving it, only letting it be a real question, as the brothers did at that table.

wordCard.voice: Ivan's rebellion. In The Brothers Karamazov, his refusal of any harmony bought with a child's tears. A question the novel lets stand. Today's word.
